messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Amina, a 30-year-old African American school counselor, had been with her husband for six years and was known at work for being calm with students, patient, and organized. Before the traumatic event, she had taken pride in being the person others came to when a child was overwhelmed or a parent needed help thinking through a problem. That sense of steadiness changed after a police encounter that began as an ordinary evening and turned frightening with alarming speed. She had been driving home when she was pulled over, and the situation escalated in a way she still replayed in fragments: the officer’s sudden commands, the harsh sound of his voice, the way he approached her vehicle, and the smell of alcohol on his breath. What stood out most to Amina was how quickly the scene shifted from routine to threat, leaving her feeling trapped, intensely watched, and certain that one wrong move could make everything worse. The force of the moment stayed with her not as a tidy story but as a series of vivid impressions, especially the sound of loud voices and abrupt movements, which she had come to associate with the sense that danger could appear without warning.

In the weeks that followed, Amina noticed that her body stayed on alert even after the event was over. She became especially watchful whenever someone moved suddenly near her, and she would tense before she even had time to think, as though her body had decided that sudden movement meant trouble. In public places and even at home, she found herself scanning doors, windows, and the people around her, unable to settle. She described feeling as if she could not truly relax anywhere, including in her own house, where she and her husband had once been able to unwind together in the evenings. Sleep did not restore her sense of safety, and on days when she felt very tired or exhausted, the world seemed even less manageable; fatigue left her feeling more exposed and less able to keep herself together. Loud noises, especially sharp bangs or abrupt sounds in the school building, brought an immediate jolt of alarm. A door slamming in the hallway or students erupting unexpectedly in the cafeteria could send her attention snapping outward, her body ready before she had any chance to decide what was happening.

Amina also began arranging her life around the hope of not being overwhelmed by feeling. She started avoiding situations that might bring on strong emotions, not because she wanted to be distant from everything, but because emotional intensity felt dangerous and hard to contain. She also found herself pulling back from situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, a pattern that confused even her because those were the moments other people seemed to seek. She said that when she let herself imagine good things, she became aware of how vulnerable she felt, as though relief could be taken away just as quickly as it had before. Over time, she began avoiding other people more broadly, turning down invitations and keeping conversation at work focused on practical matters. This had consequences in her daily life: at school, she spent less time with colleagues after hours and became more likely to eat lunch alone in her office, choosing privacy over the social rhythm that had once made her feel connected. At home, her husband noticed that she was less available for gatherings and less interested in plans that involved crowds or too much emotional energy. Amina did not describe this withdrawal as easy; it felt more like a careful shrinking of her world.

Certain reminders continued to catch her off guard. The smell of alcohol was especially upsetting, because it took her back instantly to that police encounter and to the sense that something was already wrong before she could fully understand it. The smell could appear in ordinary settings, such as a restaurant or a family event, and she would feel a sudden tightening in her chest and a wish to leave. In those moments, she often told herself that she needed to get away before she lost control of her composure. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person for not being able to “move on” like other people seemed to. She felt isolated and set apart, as though everyone else belonged to a world she could no longer fully enter. She also blamed herself for the event, believing it happened because of the way she acted during the stop, and she had spent months mentally reviewing what she might have done differently. That self-blame made it difficult for her to speak about what happened, even with her husband, because saying it aloud meant confronting the possibility that she had failed in some essential way.

By the time she sought help, Amina was exhausted by the effort of staying guarded. She was still functioning at work, but with less ease and more strain, and she no longer recognized herself in the way she moved through the day. What finally brought her to treatment was the realization that she was living as though danger might return at any moment, while also feeling cut off from the closeness and hope that had once felt natural to her. She came hoping to understand why she remained so on edge, why she kept pulling away from people and from moments that might lift her spirits, and why the memory of that night still made her feel responsible and somehow damaged. More than anything, she wanted to believe that she could feel safe again without having to keep herself braced for the worst.
